prompt: In `first.go`, the mirror answered at 80 ms and the primary at 120 ms. What did the `select` do with the primary's case?
hint: A `select` performs one case and ends.

choices.text: Ran it 40 ms later, after the mirror's
choices.why: A `select` runs one case. A second answer needs a second `select`.

choices.text: Nothing: it was not taken
choices.why: Right. The mirror's case ran and the `select` was over.

choices.text: Cancelled the primary goroutine's work
choices.why: Nothing cancels a goroutine from outside; the primary went on and sent into its buffer.

choices.text: Combined both answers into one
choices.why: Each case receives from one channel; nothing merges them.

prompt: Why do both channels in `first.go` have a buffer of one?
hint: What happens to the loser's send?

choices.text: So the `select` can see which one is ready
choices.why: A `select` sees ready sends and receives on unbuffered channels just as well.

choices.text: Because `select` refuses unbuffered channels
choices.why: It accepts any channel.

choices.text: So the loser's send completes
choices.why: Right. Nobody receives the slower answer; with room for it, the send completes anyway.

choices.text: To make the mirror answer faster
choices.why: The buffer has no effect on how long `ask` sleeps.

prompt: `fair.go` kept both channels ready and ran `select` 10,000 times: `map[a:4932 b:5068]`. What does that tell you about the order of cases?
hint: If the first case written were preferred, what would the map show?

choices.text: The first case written wins slightly more often
choices.why: `b`, the second case, won more in this run, and the next run went the other way.

choices.text: Written order gives no priority
choices.why: Right. Uniformly at random, so a busy channel cannot starve another.

choices.text: The runtime alternates between the two cases
choices.why: Strict alternation would give exactly 5000 each.

choices.text: Channel `b` is faster than channel `a`
choices.why: The two are identical; the split changes from run to run.

hint: It is used as a `case` in a `select`.

choices.text: A boolean that turns true after 200 ms
choices.why: A boolean could not be waited on by `select`.

choices.text: Nothing; it blocks the caller for 200 ms
choices.why: That is `time.Sleep`. `time.After` returns at once.

choices.text: A channel that delivers one value after 200 ms
choices.why: Right. A receive on it is the timeout case.

choices.text: An error once 200 ms have passed
choices.why: No error is involved; a value arrives on a channel.

prompt: `timeout.go` printed `timed out` after 200 ms, while its slow goroutine needed 500 ms. What happened to that goroutine?
hint: A timeout stops the waiting, not the work.

choices.text: It was stopped when the timer fired
choices.why: Nothing stopped it. Stopping work is what `context` adds, in lesson 10.

choices.text: It slept on, sent into its buffer and returned
choices.why: Right. The buffer of one let it finish even though nobody read the result.

choices.text: It panicked, because its channel had been abandoned
choices.why: There is no such thing as an abandoned channel; a send waits or completes.

choices.text: It became the result of the next `select`
choices.why: There was no next `select`; the program printed the time and ended.

prompt: A loop receives results with `case <-time.After(150 * time.Millisecond)` inside it. The source sends one result every 140 ms, forever. When does the loop time out?
hint: Each pass of the `select` creates a new timer.

choices.text: After 150 ms
choices.why: The first result arrives at 140 ms, and the next pass starts a fresh 150 ms.

choices.text: After about a second, when the timers add up
choices.why: Timers do not add up; each one is new and each is beaten.

choices.text: Never: each result beats its fresh timer
choices.why: Right. A per-step limit only catches a stream that goes quiet for longer than the limit.

choices.text: After 150 results
choices.why: The number 150 is milliseconds, and nothing counts results.

prompt: In `budget.go` the deadline made once before the loop was 350 ms, and results arrived every 100 ms. How many results did that loop get?
Inside a `for` loop with a `select`, why does `budget.go` write `break perStep` rather than `break`?

choices.text: A plain `break` would leave only the `select`
choices.why: Right. The label makes it leave the `for` loop around it.

choices.text: A plain `break` is not allowed inside `select`
choices.why: It is allowed; it just ends the `select`, and the loop goes round again.

choices.text: Labels make the loop run faster
choices.why: A label changes where control goes, not speed.

choices.text: To stop the timer created by `time.After`
choices.why: The label has nothing to do with the timer.

prompt: `try.go` offered five updates to a channel with room for two, using `select` with `default`. What did it print for updates 3, 4 and 5?
hint: The buffer was full and the `select` does not wait.

choices.text: `queued`, after waiting for room
choices.why: With a `default` there is no waiting: the case that cannot proceed is skipped.

choices.text: `dropped`
choices.why: Right. No room, so `default` ran.

choices.text: A deadlock error
choices.why: Nothing ever blocked, so there was nothing to deadlock.

choices.text: `received`, straight away
choices.why: Only 1 and 2 were received, after the loop.

prompt: `time ./restless` reported `user 0m0.994s` and `time ./patient` `user 0m0.003s`, both over one second of `real` time. Roughly how many milliseconds of processor time did polling waste?
What makes a case on a nil channel useful inside a `select`?
hint: What does a receive on a nil channel do?

choices.text: It returns the zero value at once, like a closed channel
choices.why: That is a closed channel. A nil one blocks forever.

choices.text: It panics, which shows a forgotten `make`
choices.why: Sending or receiving on nil does not panic; it blocks forever. Closing a nil channel panics.

choices.text: It is never chosen, which switches its case off
choices.why: Right. `both.go` sets each input to `nil` when it closes.

choices.text: It makes the `select` pick the other cases first
choices.why: There is no priority: the nil case is never ready, so it is never a candidate.

prompt: In `both.go`, someone deletes the line `a = nil`. Input `a` closes first. What does the loop do from then on?
hint: A closed channel is always ready to receive.

choices.text: It waits only on `b`, as before
choices.why: Without `nil`, `a`'s case stays ready, returning zero and `false` on every pass.

choices.text: It panics: receive from closed channel
choices.why: Receiving from a closed channel is allowed.

choices.text: It spins, printing `a closed` again and again, and never ends
choices.why: Right: `a != nil` stays true, and the closed case keeps winning half the draws, like `restless`.

choices.text: It ends at once, because one input is done
choices.why: The loop condition needs both to be `nil`.

prompt: Match each `select` shape with what it does.
hint: One waits for the first, one gives up, one never waits.

pairs.right: waits for whichever is ready first
sends now or not at all

pairs.left: a receive on a nil channel
pairs.right: a case that can never be chosen

right_distractors: receives from every channel in order

prompt: Put the steps of `select` in the order the lesson describes them.
hint: It looks at every case before choosing.
items: if some are ready, pick one of them at random
if none is ready and there is a `default`, run it
otherwise wait until one becomes ready

prompt: A receive on a ___ channel blocks forever, which is why setting a channel variable to it switches its case off.
hint: The zero value of a channel variable.

prompt: A worker must handle messages from `urgent` before any from `normal` whenever both are waiting. Writing the `urgent` case first in one `select` does not do it. What does?

choices.text: A larger buffer on `urgent`
choices.why: A buffer changes when a send waits, not which ready case `select` picks.

choices.text: First a `select` on `urgent` alone with a `default`, then the general one
choices.why: Right. The first `select` takes an urgent message if there is one, and only then are both considered.

choices.text: Listing `urgent` twice in the same `select`
choices.why: It would shift the odds, not give a priority: `normal` could still be chosen while urgent ones wait.

choices.text: Setting `GOMAXPROCS` to 1
choices.why: The choice among ready cases is random on any number of processors.

prompt: A progress bar goroutine reads from `updates`, and the worker must never be held up by it. Which send fits?
hint: Dropping a progress percentage is acceptable.

choices.text: `updates <- p`, on an unbuffered channel
choices.why: That waits for the progress bar every time.

choices.text: `updates <- p` in a loop with `time.Sleep` until it succeeds
choices.why: That is the worker waiting, in a slower form.

choices.text: A `select` with `case updates <- p` and a `default`
choices.why: Right. It sends if the bar is ready and drops the update otherwise.

choices.text: A `select` with `case updates <- p` and a nil channel
choices.why: A nil case is never chosen, so this waits exactly like a plain send.
